title: Earth's Systems and People
bigQuestion: How do Earth's land, water, air and living things work together, and how do people change them?

story.title: The River Chicago Turned Around
story.kicker: For fifty years the city's own waste flowed into its drinking water, until engineers made a river run the other way.
paragraphs: In the 1800s, Chicago grew faster than almost any city on Earth. Stockyards, factories and hundreds of thousands of people all dumped their waste into the Chicago River. The river was slow and flat. It carried that mess a mile east and poured it straight into Lake Michigan.

Lake Michigan was also where Chicago got its drinking water. Pipes ran out to intake cribs sitting in the lake, about 2 miles offshore. On bad days the river's filth reached the cribs anyway. People drank it. Diseases like typhoid and cholera swept through the city and killed thousands.

The city tried a canal in the 1870s, but it was too small. So engineers planned something bigger. They would dig a channel 28 miles long, deep and wide. It would run from the river southwest toward the Des Plaines River. If it were deep enough, the Chicago River would flow away from the lake instead of into it.

Thousands of workers dug for eight years with steam shovels and dynamite. On January 2, 1900, they broke the last dam. Lake water rushed into the channel. The Chicago River, for the first time, flowed backward, away from Lake Michigan, toward the Mississippi River and the Gulf of Mexico.

It worked. The drinking water got cleaner, and the disease outbreaks faded. But the waste did not vanish. It just went somewhere else, down the Illinois River, past other towns. That is the pattern of this chapter: land, water, air and living things are connected, and every change people make moves through all of them.
story.think: Reversing the river helped Chicago but sent waste toward towns downstream. Was it a good solution? What would you have wanted to know before deciding?

lessons.title: Naming the Spheres
lessons.mainIdea: Scientists divide Earth into four systems: the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere.
reading: Stand on a beach. Under your feet is sand and, below that, rock. That is the *geosphere*, all of Earth's rock and soil, from mountains to the hot center. In front of you is water. That is the *hydrosphere*: oceans, lakes, rivers, ice, and water underground.

Over your head is air. That is the *atmosphere*, the blanket of gases wrapped around Earth. And the gulls, the seaweed, the crabs, and you are the *biosphere*: every living thing on the planet. Four systems, and you are standing in all of them at once.

Scientists split Earth into these four parts to study them. But the parts are never really separate. Rain from the atmosphere falls on the geosphere and joins the hydrosphere. A plant drinks it. The trick to understanding Earth is watching how the four spheres act on each other.

words.d: all of Earth's rock, soil and the hot layers inside the planet
all of Earth's water: oceans, lakes, rivers, ice and water underground
the layer of air that surrounds Earth
every living thing on Earth, from bacteria to whales

look.title: Sorting the Backyard
look.text: A student lists what she sees in her backyard: a maple tree, a puddle, a robin, a pile of gravel, a cloud, wet mud, an earthworm, and the wind bending the grass. She tries to put each one into just one sphere. The mud and the cloud give her trouble.
look.prompt: Which items belong to more than one sphere? Why is wet mud hard to sort?

check.q: Which sphere includes lakes, oceans and ice?
check.why: Hydro means water. The hydrosphere is all of Earth's water in any form.

check.q: A robin, a worm and a maple tree all belong to which sphere?
check.why: The biosphere is every living thing on Earth.

check.q: Why do scientists say the four spheres are not really separate?
choices: They are all made of rock
They only touch at the beach
They constantly act on one another
check.why: Rain, roots, wind and waves show the spheres always affecting each other.

lessons.title: Where the Spheres Meet
lessons.mainIdea: Earth's systems constantly interact: air moves water, water shapes rock, rock feeds plants, and living things change all three.
reading: Watch the wind on Lake Michigan. Moving air (atmosphere) pushes the water (hydrosphere) into waves. The waves pound the shore and grind rock into sand (geosphere). Beach grass (biosphere) takes root in that sand and holds it against the next storm. Four spheres, one beach.

Living things are surprising movers. Tree roots crack rock. Earthworms turn soil. Tiny ocean creatures build shells that pile into limestone. Plants take carbon dioxide out of the air and put oxygen back. Over billions of years, life has changed the whole atmosphere.

The naturalist John Muir put it simply, more than a century ago. Try to pick out anything by itself, he wrote, and you find it hitched to everything else. That is the big idea of Earth science. Change one sphere and you change the others.

words.d: to act on each other; when one thing changes another and is changed back
a person who studies plants, animals and the land by careful watching

look.title: Hitched to Everything
look.text: When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the Universe.
look.cite: John Muir, My First Summer in the Sierra, 1911
look.prompt: Pick one thing in your neighborhood, such as a tree or a storm drain. What is it 'hitched to' in each of the four spheres?

check.q: Wind pushes lake water into waves that grind rock into sand. Which spheres are interacting?
check.why: Air moves water, and water changes rock: three spheres acting on each other.

check.q: How have plants changed the atmosphere over time?
choices: They take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen
They have added water to it
check.why: Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air and put oxygen back, changing what air is made of.

check.q: What did John Muir mean by 'hitched to everything else'?
choices: Everything is tied together with rope
Every part of nature is connected to the others
check.why: Muir meant that you cannot change one part of nature without touching the rest.

lessons.title: The Air Around Us
lessons.mainIdea: The atmosphere is a thin layer of mixed gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, that makes life on Earth possible.
reading: Air is not one thing. It is a mix of gases. About 78 percent is *nitrogen*, which does very little in your body. About 21 percent is *oxygen*, the part you need with every breath. Less than 1 percent is everything else, including carbon dioxide, the gas plants use to grow.

The atmosphere seems endless, but it is thin. Most of the air sits in the bottom 10 miles. Jets fly near the top of that. Compared with the whole Earth, the atmosphere is like the skin on an apple. It is that thin, and it is all we have.

That thin layer does a lot. It holds in warmth at night so Earth does not freeze. It blocks the sun's most harmful rays. It carries water from the ocean to the land as rain. And it moves. Wind is the atmosphere on the go, mixing warm and cold air across the planet.

words.d: the gas that makes up most of the air; about 78 percent
the gas in air that animals and people need to breathe; about 21 percent
a gas in the air that plants take in to grow; a very small part of the air

look.title: What Air Is Made Of
look.prompt: Carbon dioxide is a tiny part of the air, yet every plant depends on it. What does that tell you about how small amounts can matter?

check.q: Which gas makes up most of the air?
check.why: About 78 percent of dry air is nitrogen.

check.q: Why is the atmosphere compared to the skin of an apple?
choices: It is very thin compared with the whole Earth
check.why: Most air is within about 10 miles of the ground, a thin layer on a planet 8,000 miles wide.

check.q: What would happen at night if Earth had no atmosphere?
choices: The ground would lose heat and get very cold
check.why: The atmosphere holds in warmth. Without it, heat would escape quickly into space.

lessons.title: A Watery World
lessons.mainIdea: Almost all of Earth's water is salty ocean; only a tiny share is the fresh water people can drink.
reading: From space, Earth is blue. Oceans cover about 70 percent of its surface. If you added up all the water on the planet, about 97 percent of it would be *salt water* in the seas. You cannot drink it. Crops cannot grow with it. It would take a huge amount of energy to remove the salt.

The other 3 percent is *fresh water*. That sounds small, and it is. Most of it is locked away too. About two thirds of the fresh water is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers in Antarctica and Greenland. Most of the rest is underground, in the tiny spaces between grains of rock and soil.

Lakes and rivers are the water you can see. They hold only a sliver of Earth's fresh water. Yet that sliver is what most people and animals drink. A graph of Earth's water is a lesson. It shows how precious the drinkable part is.

words.d: water with salt mixed in, like the ocean; not safe to drink
water with very little salt, the kind in lakes, rivers, ice and underground

look.title: All the Water on Earth
look.prompt: If all of Earth's water were 100 buckets, how many would be drinkable fresh water you can see in lakes and rivers? What does that mean for how we use it?

check.q: About what share of Earth's water is salty ocean water?
check.why: Roughly 97 percent of all water on Earth is in the oceans.

check.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
choices: Frozen in ice sheets and glaciers
check.why: About two thirds of fresh water is frozen in Antarctica, Greenland and mountain glaciers.

check.q: Why can't people simply drink ocean water when fresh water runs short?
choices: The ocean is too far away
There is not enough of it
It is salty and removing salt takes a lot of energy
check.why: Salt makes ocean water unsafe to drink, and taking the salt out is costly.

lessons.title: Water Under Your Feet
lessons.mainIdea: Groundwater fills the spaces in rock and soil underground and is where many towns get their drinking water.
reading: Dig a hole in wet ground and it slowly fills with water. That water was already there, in the tiny gaps between soil grains and in cracks in rock. It is *groundwater*. Rain and melting snow soak down into the ground and fill those spaces from the bottom up.

The top of the water-filled zone is the *water table*. A well is just a pipe drilled below it. Many Illinois towns far from Lake Michigan drink groundwater. Farmers pump it for crops. Springs are places where the water table meets the surface and water flows out on its own.

Groundwater moves very slowly, sometimes only a few feet a year. That means it refills slowly too. Pump out more than the rain puts back and the water table drops. Wells go dry. Spill chemicals on the ground and they can reach the groundwater and stay for decades.

words.d: water that fills the spaces in soil and rock underground
the top of the underground zone where all the spaces are full of water
a hole or pipe drilled down into the ground to reach water

look.title: Earth's Fresh Water Only
look.prompt: Ice and groundwater together are 99 percent of fresh water. Which of those two is easier for people to use, and what is one risk of using it?

check.q: What is groundwater?
choices: Water filling spaces in soil and rock underground
Water on the ground after rain
check.why: Groundwater is stored in the tiny gaps between grains of soil and cracks in rock.

check.q: What happens if a town pumps out groundwater faster than rain refills it?
choices: The water table drops and wells can go dry
check.why: Groundwater refills slowly, so heavy pumping lowers the water table.

check.q: Why is a chemical spill on farmland a long-term problem?
choices: Rain washes it away in a day
It can soak into slow-moving groundwater and stay for decades
check.why: Groundwater moves very slowly, so pollution that reaches it lingers a long time.

lessons.title: The Lake Next Door
lessons.mainIdea: The Great Lakes hold about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water, and Chicago drinks from Lake Michigan every day.
reading: Chicago sits beside one of the largest supplies of fresh water on Earth. There are five *Great Lakes*. Together they hold about one fifth of the world's surface fresh water. Lake Michigan is the only one that lies entirely inside the United States.

Chicago's drinking water comes from the lake. Pipes reach out to intake cribs about 2 miles from shore. Water is pumped to treatment plants, cleaned, and sent through thousands of miles of pipe to homes in the city and many suburbs. Turn on a tap and you are drinking the lake.

The lake gives, but it also needs protection. Waste, road salt and fertilizer washed from streets and farms all end up there. Rules now limit what can go in, and the water is far cleaner than it was in 1900. Keeping it that way is a job that never ends.

words.d: five huge fresh-water lakes between the United States and Canada; Lake Michigan is one
a place where water is cleaned before it goes to homes, or after it leaves them

look.title: One Bucket of Lake
look.text: Imagine all the fresh water sitting on the surface of the whole planet, every lake and river on every continent, poured into five buckets. About one of those buckets would be the Great Lakes alone. Chicago, Milwaukee and dozens of other cities drink from that bucket every day.
look.prompt: Why might people in the Great Lakes region feel a special responsibility for this water? What could threaten it?

check.q: About how much of the world's surface fresh water is in the Great Lakes?
check.why: The five lakes together hold roughly 20 percent of the world's surface fresh water.

check.q: Where does Chicago's tap water come from?
check.why: Intake cribs about 2 miles offshore pull water from Lake Michigan for the city.

check.q: Which of these can pollute the lake after a rainstorm?
choices: Road salt and fertilizer washing off streets and fields
check.why: Runoff carries salt, fertilizer and other waste from land into the lake.

lessons.title: Making a River Run Backward
lessons.mainIdea: In 1900 Chicago reversed its river to protect its drinking water, an engineering fix that moved the problem downstream.
reading: The story that opened this chapter is a lesson in systems. Chicago's waste went into the river (hydrosphere). The river went into the lake. The lake was the drinking water. Sick people (biosphere) were the result. The problem ran through every sphere.

The fix was to dig. The Sanitary and Ship Canal, opened in January 1900, was deep enough that water flowed out of the lake and into the canal. The river's direction *reversed*. Waste now traveled southwest, toward the Illinois River and the Mississippi.

Chicago's drinking water got safer. But towns along the Illinois River got the waste. Later, Chicago built treatment plants to clean the water before it left the city. Today the city also has the Deep Tunnel, more than 100 miles of huge tunnels that hold storm water until plants can clean it.

words.d: to turn around and go the opposite way
a channel dug by people for water or boats to travel through
in the direction a river flows; farther along the river

look.title: The Town Down the River
look.text: It is 1901. You live in a small town on the Illinois River, 100 miles southwest of Chicago. Your town fishes the river and draws some water from it. Since last year the river smells worse, especially in summer. A newspaper says Chicago's new canal sends the big city's waste your way.
look.prompt: Chicago's problem was solved. Was yours created? What would you ask engineers to add to their design?

check.q: Why did Chicago reverse its river?
choices: To keep sewage out of its drinking water in Lake Michigan
To fill the river with lake fish
check.why: Waste in the river had been flowing into the lake, the city's water source, causing disease.

check.q: After 1900, where did Chicago's river water go?
choices: Toward the Illinois and Mississippi Rivers
check.why: The canal carried the water southwest, toward the Illinois River and eventually the Gulf of Mexico.

check.q: What is the main lesson of the reversal for people who change Earth's systems?
choices: A fix in one place can send the problem somewhere else
check.why: Chicago got cleaner water, but the waste moved downstream to other towns.

lessons.title: Using What Earth Gives
lessons.mainIdea: People use Earth's resources for food, energy and materials, and that use changes the land, water and air.
reading: Everything you own came from Earth. Your desk was a tree. Your phone holds metals dug from rock. The lights run on electricity, much of it made by burning coal or gas pulled from underground. These are *natural resources*: things from Earth that people use.

Illinois is rich in resources. Its deep black soil grows more corn and soybeans than almost any state. Coal lies under much of the southern half. Rivers and the lake carry ships. But using resources changes the land. When settlers arrived, tall prairie grass covered most of Illinois. Today only tiny scraps of that prairie remain.

Some resources grow back. Trees, crops and clean water are *renewable* if we do not use them faster than they return. Coal, oil and metals do not grow back on any human timescale. They are *nonrenewable*. Once burned or used, they are gone. That difference shapes how carefully each should be used.

words.d: something from Earth that people use, like water, soil, wood, coal or metal
able to grow back or be replaced in a person's lifetime, like trees or crops
used up faster than Earth can make more, like coal or oil

look.title: The Prairie Under the Corn
look.text: In 1820, a traveler crossing central Illinois saw grass taller than a man, stretching to the horizon, with flowers and prairie chickens and bison trails. Today the same spot is a corn field, a road, and a grain elevator. The soil the corn grows in was built by that prairie over thousands of years.
look.prompt: What did people gain by plowing the prairie? What was lost, and can it be replaced?

check.q: Which of these is a nonrenewable resource?
check.why: Coal took millions of years to form and does not grow back once burned.

check.q: Why is Illinois soil so good for farming?
choices: Glaciers and thousands of years of prairie built it
Farmers add it from other states
check.why: Ground-up rock from the glaciers plus ages of rotting prairie grass made deep, rich soil.

check.q: When is a forest a renewable resource?
choices: When trees are cut faster than they grow
When no trees are ever cut
When trees grow back as fast as they are used
check.why: A resource is renewable only if it is replaced as fast as people use it.

lessons.title: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
lessons.mainIdea: Using less, using things again, and recycling materials all save resources and cut waste.
reading: Every can, bottle and box takes resources to make and energy to move. When it is thrown away, it goes to a *landfill*, a giant pit that is covered when full. Landfills take up land and can leak into groundwater. Three habits shrink what goes there: reduce, reuse, recycle.

Reduce means use less in the first place: a refillable bottle instead of a new one each day. Reuse means use the same thing again: a jar becomes a pencil cup. *Recycle* means send the material back to a factory to become something new. Old paper becomes new paper. Old cans become new cans.

Recycling saves more than space. Making a can from recycled aluminum uses about 95 percent less energy than making one from raw ore. But recycling is not free either. Trucks, sorting and cleaning all take energy. That is why 'reduce' comes first on the list.

words.d: a large pit where trash is buried and covered
to send a used material back to be made into something new
to use something carefully so it lasts

look.title: The Lunchroom Trash Can
look.text: A class weighs their lunchroom trash for a week: 40 pounds a day. Half of it is uneaten food. A quarter is plastic bottles and cans. The rest is paper and wrappers. They try changes: a share table for unopened food, a recycling bin, and water refill stations. The next week the trash weighs 18 pounds a day.
look.prompt: Which change probably made the biggest difference, and which of the three Rs was it?

check.q: Which of the three Rs does the most good, and why does it come first?
choices: Reduce, because using less means nothing has to be made or thrown away
Reuse, because jars make good cups
check.why: Not using something in the first place saves all the energy and material it would have taken.

check.q: Using a jar as a pencil cup is an example of
check.why: Reuse means using the same object again for something.

check.q: Why does recycling aluminum save so much energy?
choices: Melting old cans takes far less energy than making metal from raw ore
Recycled cans do not need trucks
check.why: Recycled aluminum skips the energy-hungry step of pulling metal from ore, saving about 95 percent.

lessons.title: Protecting Earth's Systems
lessons.mainIdea: People can repair some of the damage they cause, using science to protect water, land, air and living things.
reading: People change Earth, but people can also protect it. In 1970, millions of Americans marked the first *Earth Day*. Soon after, laws limited what factories could put into rivers and the air. Rivers that once caught fire from pollution now have fish again. Chicago's river is one of them.

Illinois groups are bringing back the prairie. They collect seeds from surviving patches and plant them on old fields and along highways. Deep roots return. Butterflies and birds follow. It takes years, but a piece of the biosphere that was almost gone is growing back.

Protecting Earth's systems is not about stopping all use. People need food, water, energy and homes. It is about *stewardship*: using resources wisely so they last, measuring the effects, and fixing problems when the evidence shows them. Every one of the four spheres is in your care.

words.d: a day each April, first held in 1970, when people work to protect the planet
taking care of something so it stays healthy for the future
to bring something back to the way it was

look.title: A President on Conservation
look.text: In 1908, President Theodore Roosevelt called the nation's governors to the White House to talk about natural resources. He told them that caring for the country's forests, water, soil and minerals was one of the most important problems the nation faced, because those resources were the foundation of everything else.
look.cite: Theodore Roosevelt, opening address to the Conference of Governors on conservation, 1908
look.prompt: Roosevelt spoke before cars were common and long before Earth Day. Why might he have worried about resources so early?

check.q: What happened after laws limited pollution in rivers?
choices: Fish and other life returned to many rivers
check.why: Cleaner water allowed fish and other living things to come back, including in the Chicago River.

check.q: How do people restore prairie in Illinois?
choices: By planting seeds gathered from surviving prairie patches
check.why: Seeds from the last natural patches are planted on old fields, and the prairie slowly grows back.

check.q: What does stewardship of Earth's systems mean?
choices: Using resources wisely and fixing problems the evidence shows
Using resources as fast as possible
check.why: Stewardship means careful use, measuring effects, and repairing harm, not stopping all use.

review.q: Which sphere is the layer of air around Earth?
review.why: The atmosphere is the blanket of gases surrounding the planet.

review.q: Tree roots crack a boulder. Which two spheres are interacting?
review.why: A living thing, the tree, is changing rock, part of the geosphere.

review.q: About what share of Earth's water is fresh?
review.why: Only about 3 percent of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is ice or underground.

review.q: Which gas is about 21 percent of the air and needed for breathing?
review.why: Oxygen is about a fifth of the air and is what animals need with each breath.

review.q: Why was Chicago's river reversed in 1900?
choices: To keep waste out of the city's drinking water
To make the river deeper for fish
review.why: Sewage had been flowing into Lake Michigan, the source of Chicago's drinking water.
Trees grow back within a human lifetime if they are not cut faster than they regrow.

review.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
review.why: About two thirds of fresh water is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers.

review.q: A town pumps groundwater faster than rain refills it. What will likely happen?
review.why: Groundwater refills slowly, so heavy pumping lowers the water table until wells run dry.
